How to read a scoreboard and results

In clay shooting the score is simple: the number of targets broken. A round is 25 targets in both Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting, and an international competition is 200 targets, shot in rounds of 25. So the highest possible score is 200 out of 200.

Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™

Each target ends up on a score card. In Sporting™ the referee keeps the card, or someone working under the referee’s eye. On the standard FITASC card each target is listed by the letter of its trap (A, B, C…), with X for a hit and O for a miss. The card also has a total and a column for signatures. Before the squad moves to the next stand, the referee photographs the card.

Where this is in the rules: Chapter 14 · Scorecard model

Compak® Sporting

In Compak® Sporting shot by squad the referee keeps the score sheet and marks a hit X and a miss O. The referee announces each zero aloud or with a sound signal, so that a shooter who disagrees can protest at once. In Compak in line, where an approved electronic system records the scores (electronic refereeing), the results appear on a screen.

Where this is in the rules: Chapter 15 · Announcing zeros; marks O and X

In Sporting™ you must check your score when you leave each stand. If you disagree with a mark, tell the referee at once: the referee decides, perhaps after asking others, and that decision cannot be appealed. In Compak® Sporting you sign the score sheet at the end of the round; if you refuse to sign, you lose the right to complain.

At international events the round scores go to a central scoreboard or an electronic system. Next to each name you usually see the score of each round and the total. So you can see not only who is leading, but also who shoots steadily and who had a bad round.

Equal totals are common. Ties for the first three places are settled by a shoot-off of 25 targets, then sudden death if the scores are still level (in sudden death the first shooter to miss is out). Below third place tied shooters share the place, and countback sets their order in the list. How both work: Categories, classes and shoot-offs.

Besides the open ranking there are categories, such as Junior, Lady, Senior and Veteran, and a team ranking. So a prize giving can have several winners, one in each ranking.

After a competition the results appear on ClayArena. The table shows each shooter’s place and the number of targets broken. From there you can open the shooter profile, with their competitions and figures such as accuracy and best score. More: How to find your results and your profile.

Tip: Compare scores only over the same number of targets, and preferably from the same event: layouts at different grounds differ in difficulty. 90 out of 100 and 180 out of 200 are the same percentage, but a longer event is a different test.

Key points

  • The score is the number of targets broken; an international event is 200 targets, shot in rounds of 25.
  • X = hit, O = miss on FITASC score cards
  • Sporting™: check your score when leaving each stand; Compak® Sporting: sign the sheet or lose the right to complain
  • Categories and the team ranking mean several winners at one prize giving.
  • Compare scores over the same number of targets, preferably from the same event.

Did you know?

In Sporting™ each stand of a layout has its own pencil colour on the score card. When the squad moves on, an asterisk marks the shooter who carries the card to the next stand.

Stand Talk

  • Referee Check your card before you leave the stand.

    Meaning: Sporting™: look at your marks now; later objections are not accepted.

  • Referee Sign here, please.

    Meaning: Compak® Sporting: signing confirms the score; refusing means losing the right to complain.

  • Referee Twenty-three — you dropped two.

    Meaning: Score 23 of 25; two targets were lost.

For the interpreter
  • Translate “check your card” as an urgent instruction, not a polite remark: once the shooter has left the stand, a wrong mark can no longer be challenged.

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. On a FITASC score card, what does O mean?

    1. A hit
    2. A No Bird
    3. A miss
    4. An empty stand
    Answer

    A miss

    On the standard FITASC card a hit is marked X and a miss O.

    Chapter 14 · Scorecard model

  2. In Compak® Sporting your shooter refuses to sign the score sheet. What is the consequence?

    1. He loses the right to make any complaint
    2. The round is shot again
    3. The referee signs and nothing changes
    4. He gets 25 zeros automatically
    Answer

    He loses the right to make any complaint

    The Compak® Sporting rules say a shooter who refuses to sign loses the right to complain.

    Chapter 15 · Signing the score sheet

  3. You want to compare the scores of two shooters. What is a fair way to do it?

    1. Compare the percentages, whatever the length of the event
    2. Compare only the highest round each of them shot
    3. Compare them over the same number of targets, preferably at one event
    Answer

    Compare them over the same number of targets, preferably at one event

    The same percentage over a different number of targets, or at other grounds, is not the same test: layouts differ in difficulty.
